notes:
Here is a verse-by-verse commentary on Jeremiah 48:25–47, drawn from the allowed sources. Each point is followed by its URL.

---

## v. 25 — “The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm is broken,” declares the LORD.

- **The horn** is the symbol of strength drawn from horned animals; “arm” represents human power to grasp sword or sceptre. Together they mean Moab’s total loss of defensive and offensive capability. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Trapp adds that “horn” stands for “his strength, power, glory, kingdoms; his sultans and princes, saith the Chaldee.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html
- Guzik notes that horn and arm represent strength from the animal world and the human world respectively; God would show Moab empty of all strength. (Guzik/EnduringWord) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- The Pulpit Commentary sees this verse capping the long list of doomed cities (vv. 21–24): Moab’s power is now gone. (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 26 — “Make him drunk, because he has magnified himself against the LORD; so Moab will wallow in his own vomit, and he will also become a laughingstock.”

- The command “Make him drunk” is addressed to the agents of divine wrath (Babylon). The drunkenness is “a dry drunkenness with the fierce wrath of God” — the cup of Yahweh’s fury from Jeremiah 25:15–29. (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html
- Ellicott notes the image is “suggested by the wine-cup of Jehovah’s fury … as men looked with scorn on the drunkard wallowing in his shame, so should they look on Moab.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik observes that the Hebrew verb *sapaq* (translated “wallow”) actually means “to clap the hands” or “clap the thigh,” so “presumably the reference here is to a person holding his abdomen as he vomits.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary emphasises that Moab is made drunk “not with wine, but by the terror of the Lord” and will be mocked as he had mocked Israel. (Garner-Howes Baptist) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-48.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says Moab’s offence is “haughty contempt of Jehovah,” and the coarse figure is “not unnatural in the oratory … of a rude people like the Jews.” (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 27 — “Was not Israel your object of ridicule? Was he ever found among thieves? For whenever you speak of him you shake your head.”

- Ellicott explains: the question “Was he found among thieves?” expects the answer “No.” Israel had not been among the lawless, aggressive nations. Moab’s derision was therefore unjustified. The “shaking of the head” is a gesture of triumphant malice. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Trapp: Moab composed “comedies out of his tragedies” when Israel was taken captive by Assyria. The rhetorical question means, “What reason hadst thou to shout after him, as one would do after a thief that is taken stealing?” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html
- Matthew Henry notes that Moab’s contempt for God’s people is a chief cause of judgment. (Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-48.html
- The Pulpit Commentary renders the sense: “What giveth thee the right to show such scorn and insolent triumph towards Israel, as if he were one who had been arrested in the very act of robbery?” (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 28 — “Abandon the towns and settle among the rocks, O dwellers of Moab! Be like a dove that nests at the mouth of a cave.”

- The dove nesting in clefts of the rock is a picture of fugitives hiding in inaccessible places. Ellicott notes that the wild dove flies to “the clefts of the rock” (Song 2:14) and that caves were always the asylum of fugitives in Palestine (1 Sam 13:6; 2 Sam 17:9). (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik: “The coming judgment would make the people of Moab refugees from their cities, forced to find refuge in the mountains and their rocks.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- The Pulpit Commentary adds that Jeremiah probably thinks of the rocky defiles of the Arnon, which have “perpendicular walls of rock” ideal for fugitives. (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html
- Whedon notes: “The wild rock pigeon invariably selects deep ravines for its nesting and roosting places.” (Whedon) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 29 — “We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his proud arrogance and haughtiness of heart.”

- This verse is closely based on Isaiah 16:6. Ellicott says Jeremiah reproduces Isaiah’s words to show that “the fault of which he spoke was inveterate, and had shown itself incurable.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik notes the piling up of synonymous terms — “loftiness, arrogance, pride, haughtiness of heart” — designed to emphasise the depth of Moab’s pride. Thompson is cited: “Jeremiah here piles up a number of synonymous terms designed to emphasize Moab’s pride.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Trapp wryly observes: “Proud he was then, and the same he is still; no changeling is he.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests Moab’s boastfulness is illustrated by the Moabite Stone inscription, though “all national monuments of this sort have a tendency to exaggeration.” (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 30 — “I know his insolence,” declares the LORD, “but it is futile. His boasting is as empty as his deeds.”

- The Hebrew is difficult. The Pulpit Commentary argues that “his lies” (AV) is better understood as “the untruth of his pratings [i.e., boastings]; the untruth that they have wrought.” In word and deed Moab was essentially “untrue” — truth in the Biblical sense being to know and serve the true God. (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html
- Ellicott renders the sense: “Not so” — the sentence of frustration — “is written alike on the wrath which leads to passionate outrage, and on the lies in which it seeks to find safety.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik connects Moab’s “wrath” to their pride: “Believing themselves to be better than others, they found it easy to feel and act in an angry manner. God knew that it is not right. Their pride explained their anger but did not justify it.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Trapp: “Passion is the eldest daughter of pride.” Also notes that “lies were his refuge, his strength, the bars he trusted to and leaned on.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 31 — “Therefore I will wail for Moab; I will cry out for all of Moab; I will moan for the men of Kir-heres.”

- The “I” who wails is debated: Ellicott says it is “neither Jehovah nor the prophet, but the unnamed mourner,” possibly Jeremiah speaking in his own person in sympathy, or a representative mourner. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik: “Even though the judgment was richly deserved, it was not rejoiced in. God and His prophet would cry out and mourn.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- The Pulpit Commentary explains: “An inspired prophet has, as it were, a double personality. Sometimes his human feelings seem quite lost in the consciousness of his message; sometimes (and especially in Jeremiah) the natural, emotional life refuses to be thus restrained.” (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html
- Kir-heres (Kir-hareseth) is identified with modern Kerak, “occupying a strong position on one of the Moabite mountains to the south-east of the Dead Sea.” Its name means “City of the Sun.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm

---

## v. 32 — “I will weep for you, O vine of Sibmah, more than I weep for Jazer. Your tendrils have extended to the sea; they reach even to Jazer. The destroyer has descended on your summer fruit and grape harvest.”

- This verse echoes Isaiah 16:8–9. Sibmah was famous for vineyards that extended to Jazer. Ellicott notes that the “sea of Jazer” (if the text is right) must have been some inland lake or pond, now unidentified. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Trapp renders it: “more largely and lamentably than Isaiah bewailed Jazer.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: “with the weeping of Jazer” means “more than the weeping of Jazer,” i.e., either “more than I weep for Jazer” or “more than Jazer weeps for the devastated vineyards of Sibmah.” Jazer is located between Ramoth and Heshbon. (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html
- Guzik summarises: “Moab’s previous prosperity in the field and the winepress would turn to sorrow and desolation.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/

---

## v. 33 — “Joy and gladness are removed from the orchard and from the fields of Moab. I have stopped the flow of wine from the presses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; their shouts are not for joy.”

- The vintage-song of those who trod out the grapes is replaced by wailing, or by the shout of battle. Ellicott: “the shout … shall be turned to wailing and lamentation, or the shout and tumult of battle shall have taken its place.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik, citing Harrison: “The implication is that the shout will not be the glad cry of the vintagers, but the noise of warriors bent on destruction.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- The “I” in “I have caused wine to fail” is Jehovah speaking directly. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Trapp: “Their cheer shall be changed, their note altered … mirth shall be turned into mourning, clapping of hands into wringing of hands, hallooing into howling.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 34 — “There is a cry from Heshbon to Elealeh; they raise their voices to Jahaz, from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah; for even the waters of Nimrim have dried up.”

- The cry covers the whole land from north (Heshbon) to south (Zoar). “Eglath-shelishiyah” is rendered “like a three-year-old heifer” — Clarke explains: “which runs lowing from place to place in search of her calf, which is lost or taken from her.” (Guzik, citing Clarke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Ellicott notes the verse begins with a corrupt text in the Hebrew but the general meaning is “widespread ruin.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that this verse draws on Isaiah 15:4–5, 9. (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 35 — “In Moab, declares the LORD, I will bring an end to those who make offerings on the high places and burn incense to their gods.”

- This is a direct judgment against Moabite idolatry. Their cultic worship on the high places (bāmôt) would cease completely — partly through destruction of the shrines and partly through depopulation. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Ellicott observes that this corresponds to Isaiah 16:12 — Moab’s prayers to Chemosh would be futile. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary: “Such a scarcity there shall be of people” that no one will remain to offer sacrifices. (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 36 — “Therefore My heart laments like a flute for Moab; it laments like a flute for the men of Kir-heres, because the wealth they acquired has perished.”

- The “flute” (or pipes) was the typical instrument of mourning in the ancient Near East. God Himself is portrayed as lamenting, underscoring that judgment, even when deserved, grieves the heart of God. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Ellicott: this echoes Isaiah 16:11 — “My heart shall sound like pipes for Moab.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Matthew Henry: the prophet himself laments, showing that “judgment, even when deserved, grieves the heart of God.” (Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 37 — “For every head is shaved and every beard is clipped; on every hand is a gash, and around every waist is sackcloth.”

- These are traditional mourning rites of the East: shaving the head, cutting the beard, gashing the body, wearing sackcloth. Ellicott and others note these were also pagan practices forbidden to Israel (Lev 19:27–28; Deut 14:1), but common among Moab. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik simply notes that Jeremiah “recounted their many demonstrations of mourning.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Trapp: “This was the doings among the Easterlings, in times of mourning.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 38 — “On all the rooftops of Moab and in the public squares, everyone is mourning; for I have shattered Moab like an unwanted jar,” declares the LORD.

- Rooftops were places of public lamentation (cf. Isa 15:3). The image of a cheap clay pot “in which is no pleasure” — broken and discarded — pictures how easily and completely God would judge Moab. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Ellicott: the vessel imagery recalls Jeremiah 19:10. Clay pots were cheaply made and easily broken when no longer useful. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary: “Like a vessel wherein is no pleasure” echoes Jeremiah 22:28. (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 39 — “How shattered it is! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame! Moab has become an object of ridicule and horror to all those around him.”

- Ellicott notes the emphatic iteration: “derision” was pointedly used in vv. 26 and 27; now it comes back on Moab’s own head. The phrase “turned the back” in Hebrew is literally “turned the neck” — a picture of humiliated submission. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik: Moab, who had ridiculed Israel, now becomes the object of ridicule to surrounding nations — poetic justice. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- At this point Ellicott notes that the parallelism with Isaiah 15–16 ceases and the prediction takes “a more independent character.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm

---

## v. 40 — “For this is what the LORD says: ‘Behold, an eagle swoops down and spreads his wings against Moab.’”

- The eagle (or vulture) is Nebuchadnezzar — a natural symbol of a fierce, swift invader (Deut 28:49; Isa 46:11; Ezek 17:3). Ellicott notes the image “receives a fresh vividness from the previous comparison of Moab to the dove that had its nest in the clefts of the rock.” The eagle will easily overtake the dove. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Trapp: “To an eagle Nebuchadnezzar is compared, for his strength, swiftness, and ravenousness.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: “like an eagle, Nebuchadnezzar is about to swoop and spread his wings against Moab.” (Garner-Howes Baptist) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 41 — “Kirioth has been taken, and the strongholds seized. In that day the heart of Moab’s warriors will be like the heart of a woman in labor.”

- “Heart of a woman in labor” conveys sudden, overwhelming fear and helplessness. Warriors known for strength are reduced to panic. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Ellicott discusses whether “Kerioth” (with the article) should be translated “the cities” to paint widespread devastation rather than one specific town. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Trapp notes an interesting tradition: “Of this city, some say, was Judas Iscariot.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html
- The Pulpit Commentary identifies Kerioth as “perhaps a synonym of Ar, the old capital of Moab” (cf. Amos 2:2). (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 42 — “Moab will be destroyed as a nation because he vaunted himself against the LORD.”

- Guzik: “The people of Moab would no longer continue as a separate, defined people. In a sense they would be lost to history, unlike Israel. All this came because he exalted himself against the LORD.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Ellicott clarifies: “What is predicted is not annihilation (see v. 47), but the loss of national independence. … With Moab, as with other nations, it was her self-exalting pride that called for chastisement.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Joseph Parker: “The destruction … was not arbitrary, but moral, being based upon an assigned reason. ‘Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.’” (Parker) — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/parker/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik, citing Harrison, notes that Moab’s extinction began “with a heavy Nabatean settlement in the first century BC, and culminated under the Arabs in the Byzantine period.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/

---

## v. 43 — “Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of Moab,” declares the LORD.

- The threefold formula — “terror (or fear), pit, snare” — is taken from Isaiah 24:17–18, where it had become “something like proverbial use.” Ellicott explains the progression: first the terror of a hunted animal, then the pit dug to trap it, then the snare for those who scramble out. (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik: “God promised that the judgment to come upon Moab would be thorough. If someone escaped an aspect of it, another aspect of judgment would catch up with them.” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Matthew Henry: “There shall be fear to drive them into the pit, and a snare to hold them fast in it when they are in it.” (Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-48.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that vv. 43–44 “cohere so loosely with the context, that interpolation is a not unreasonable hypothesis,” though they serve to underscore the inescapability of judgment. (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 44 — “Whoever flees the panic will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare. For I will bring upon Moab the year of their punishment,” declares the LORD.

- The triple threat means total inescapability. “The year of their punishment” (or “visitation”) is the appointed time when God reckons with Moab. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- Matthew Henry: “It is the year of their visitation, when God comes to reckon with them.” (Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-48.html
- Peake’s Commentary (modern scholarship): “One disaster succeeds another in this time of punishment (‘visitation,’ Jeremiah 11:23, Jeremiah 23:12).” (Peake) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 45 — “Those who flee will stand helpless in Heshbon’s shadow, because fire has gone forth from Heshbon and a flame from within Sihon. It devours the foreheads of Moab and the skulls of the sons of tumult.”

- This verse quotes an ancient war-song from Numbers 21:28–29. Ellicott: “The Moabites are represented as taking refuge under the walls of Heshbon, but, instead of finding shelter, fire bursts out from walls and gates.” “Corner” and “crown of the head” symbolise total destruction (as in shaving, Isa 7:20). The “sons of tumult” are the “panic-stricken clamorous crowds of the Moabite fugitives.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik, citing Thompson: “We may see in these words a claim that Balaam’s oracle against Moab was about to be enacted.” The irony: Heshbon, once Sihon’s capital from which fire went forth against Moab in Moses’ day, now becomes the place where Moabite fugitives find no safety. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes vv. 45–46 are omitted in the Septuagint and are “evidently based on Numbers 21:28, 29.” (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 46 — “Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished; for your sons have been taken into exile and your daughters have gone into captivity.”

- This is a quotation adapted from Numbers 21:29. Chemosh, Moab’s national deity, cannot save his people. Ellicott notes the “captivity of the idol implies, of course, that of the people.” (Ellicott) — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/48.htm
- Guzik: “Chemosh was the principal Moabite deity (Numbers 21:29) and the sacrificing of children was an important part of his cult (2 Kings 3:27).” (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: “The ancient prophecy of Balaam is coming to fulfillment (comp. Numbers 21:28; 24:17).” (Garner-Howes Baptist) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-48.html

---

## v. 47 — “Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity,” declares the LORD. Here ends the judgment on Moab.

This verse is the most debated in the passage, with significantly different interpretations across traditions:

### Traditional / Older Protestant Reading (Spiritual/Messianic)
- **Matthew Henry**: “Thus tenderly does God deal with Moabites. … Yet it looks further, to gospel times; the Jews themselves refer it to the days of the Messiah; then the captivity of the Gentiles, under the yoke of sin and Satan, shall be brought back by divine grace, which shall make them free, free indeed.” (Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-48.html
- **Trapp** says this was “never that we find fulfilled in the letter, therefore it was a presage of the calling of the Gentiles to an interest in Christ, and benefit by him.” (Trapp) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/jeremiah-48.html
- **Wesley’s Explanatory Notes** (Methodist): “It seems this is to be understood of a spiritual reduction of them, by calling them into the kingdom of the Messiah.” (Wesley) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/jeremiah-48.html

### Reformed Reading (Calvin)
- **John Calvin** teaches that this promise was given not for Moab’s sake but for Israel’s: “God gives place to his mercy, so that the Moabites should not wholly perish. … Why, then, was this promise given? not for the sake of the Moabites; but that the Jews might feel assured that God would at length be propitious to them; he promises pardon to the Moabites as it were accidentally … with a design through this mercy to give to the Israelites a taste of his paternal favor.” (Calvin, via CCEL) — https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom21/calcom21.ii.i.xlv.html

### Dispensational/Futurist Reading
- **Gaebelein’s Annotated Bible**: “The last verse speaks of a territorial restoration of Moab, not of a restitution of that wicked generation, as some teach. We do not know where a remnant of Moab is today, to possess in millennial times their former land; nor do we know how the Lord is going to accomplish it. But we know He will fulfill His own Word.” (Gaebelein) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/jeremiah-48.html
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word, charismatic/Pentecostal-leaning): “Despite the complete nature of the judgment to come against them, God promised a measure of mercy to Moab in the latter days.” No further specification. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-48/

### Historical Fulfillment Reading
- **The Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary** notes: “Josephus records how the Moabites were afterwards restored to their country (Antiq., xiii. 13, §5, 14, §2), though never to their former political importance.” (Preacher’s Homiletical) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-48.html
- **Sutcliffe’s Commentary**: “Josephus in his Antiquities, Jeremiah 13:23, says that after the captivity, the Moabites were reduced under the power of the Jews, and received circumcision.” (Sutcliffe) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jsc/jeremiah-48.html

### Modern Critical Scholarship
- **Peake’s Commentary**: “Moab goes into exile, but Yahweh will ultimately change her fortunes. The closing sentence (Jeremiah 48:47) is an editorial note.” (Peake) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/jeremiah-48.html
- **The Pulpit Commentary** also regards “Thus far is the judgment of Moab” as “clearly an editor’s note (comp. Jeremiah 51:64).” (Pulpit) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-48.html
- **Bennett’s Expositor’s Bible**: “As the chapter, in its present form, concludes with a note — ‘I will bring again the captivity of Moab in the latter days — it is the utterance of Jehovah’ — we gather that even this rough handling was disciplinary.” (Bennett, CCEL) — https://ccel.org/ccel/bennett/expositorjer2/expositorjer2.vii.iv.html

### Baptist Reading
- The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** simply notes: “Yet, even in His wrath, God is merciful toward Moab; in the latter days his fortunes will be restored (comp. Jeremiah 12:14–17; 49:6, 39).” (Garner-Howes Baptist) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-48.html

### Roman Catholic and Orthodox Readings

Search limits were reached before these could be fetched. However, Peake’s Commentary (above) represents the modern critical approach, noting the composite nature of the chapter and the editorial character of v. 47b.

---

**Summary of the key interpretive divide on v. 47:** The older Protestant tradition (Henry, Trapp, Wesley) reads the restoration spiritually — as a prophecy of Gentile inclusion in the Messiah’s kingdom. Calvin sees it as a promise given for Israel’s encouragement, not primarily for Moab. Dispensational interpreters (Gaebelein) expect a literal, territorial restoration in the millennium. Some (Preacher’s Homiletical, Sutcliffe) find a partial historical fulfilment in the post-exilic period recorded by Josephus. Modern critics (Peake, Pulpit) regard the closing verse as a later editorial addition.
